title: A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams on Avian Carriers

hero.subtitle: The legendary April Fools' RFC - IP datagrams carried by homing pigeons

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Published on April 1st, 1990, RFC 1149 is one of the most beloved documents in Internet history. It specifies a method for transmitting IP datagrams using homing pigeons as the physical carrier medium.

While written as humor, RFC 1149 is a legitimate document in the RFC series. It was even implemented and tested on April 28, 2001, by the Bergen Linux User Group in Norway, achieving a 55% packet loss rate and round-trip times of thousands of seconds.
sections.eli5: This is a joke document that is also a real document. It says how you could send internet messages by bird, and a group of people once did.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
Avian carriers can provide high delay, low throughput, and low altitude service. The connection topology is limited to a single point-to-point path for each carrier, used with standard carriers, but many carriers can be used without significant interference with each other, outside of early spring.

Bandwidth
Depends on the weight capacity of the carrier and the storage medium. A pigeon carrying a microSD card could theoretically transfer terabytes per trip.
Latency
Homing pigeon speed averages 50 mph (80 km/h), giving a latency measured in hours for typical distances.
Packet Loss
Susceptible to hawks, cats, weather, and other environmental factors. The Bergen test recorded 55% packet loss.
sections.eli5: Birds are slow and carry very little, but there are lots of sky to go around, so many birds can fly at once without bumping into each other.

sections.title: Frame Format
sections.content:
The IP datagram is printed on a small scroll of paper, in hexadecimal, with each octet separated by "whitestuff and blackstuff". The scroll of paper is wrapped around one leg of the avian carrier.

Frame Format

of paper, in hexadecimal, with each octet
separated by whitestuff and blackstuff.

The scroll of paper is wrapped around one
leg of the avian carrier.

A band of duct tape is used to secure
the datagram's edges.
sections.eli5: You write the message in numbers on a little paper scroll, wrap it around the bird's leg and tape it on. At the other end someone takes the tape off and scans the paper into a computer.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.content:
The specification addresses several practical implementation concerns for deploying IP over avian carrier networks.

MTUVariable; typically 256 milligrams, and generally increasing with carrier age
BandwidthLimited to the leg length
PaddingSome datagram padding may be needed
StormsBroadcasting is not specified; storms can cause data loss

Audit trails are automatically generated, and can often be found on logs and cable trays.
sections.eli5: A bird can only carry so much, so the message has to be small, and a storm can make the bird lose it.

sections.title: Quality of Service
sections.content:
RFC 1149 itself says little about quality of service (RFC 2549 adds it), but a rough, informal comparison with Ethernet shows how different avian carriers are.

Metric
Avian Carriers
Ethernet
Latency
Hours to days
Microseconds
Bandwidth
High (if using microSD)
1-100 Gbps
Packet Loss
~55% (tested)
< 0.01%
Jitter
Very high (wind-dependent)
Very low
sections.eli5: Compared with a normal network cable, a bird is very slow and often loses the message, but it can carry a lot at once if you give it a big memory card.

references.text: Waitzman, D., "IP over Avian Carriers with Quality of Service", RFC 2549, April 1999.

subtitle: IP datagrams on a paper scroll wrapped around a bird's leg.

eli5.summary: Write your message on a small piece of paper, tape it to a bird's leg, and let the bird fly it to a friend, who copies it back into a computer.

tldr.problem: Move IP datagrams between two places that have no electronic link between them.
tldr.mechanism: Print the datagram in hexadecimal on a small paper scroll, wrap it around one leg of an avian carrier and secure it with duct tape. The receiver removes the tape and optically scans the paper back into electronic form.
tldr.outcome: It is a joke with a real number: published on 1 April 1990 as an Experimental RFC, it was extended by RFC 2549 and was actually tried by the Bergen Linux User Group in 2001.

questions: can you send ip packets by carrier pigeon
what is the mtu of an avian carrier
why was rfc 1149 published on april 1
what is the difference between rfc 1149 and rfc 2549
today: RFC 1149 is the best known of the April 1 RFCs and is cited whenever someone wants to talk about latency, packet loss or the absurd end of protocol design. The 2001 Bergen test showed that the idea works in a very literal sense, with the loss and delay figures quoted above. Its follow-up, RFC 2549, adds quality of service.
